I would not wish to use unparliamentary language towards any hon. gentleman, and especially is that the case in reference to my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson), but if his friends have seen fit to indulge in taunts against me, I have the satisfaction of knowing that they did me no harm, and as to the mystery which surrounded my silence, that seems to have worried these hon. gentlemen themselves more than it has troubled me.
And now with regard to the charge of inconsistency. We have had quires of extracts quoted to show that I have been inconsistent, and that my course during the discussion on the Bill to incorporate the Grand Trunk Pacific Company last year, was not in harmony with the course that X have since pursued. Let us see about that. Certain gentlemen were desirous of being incorporated under the name of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company with a view to construct and operate a railway between the Pacific ocean and' North Bay. i opposed that Bill in the committee. I felt that it was not a national line. I believed that it was not in the true sense a measure that would fulfil the expectations of the people in all sections of Canada. I did not take that attitude merely in the interest of the section of the country from which I come. I took it because I felt that it was in the interest of all Cfln-ada that if we were to aid any railway at all we should have a railway from the shores of the Pacific to the shores of the Atlantic, built across the continent on Canadian soil. I felt that if this line were constructed and aided by government subsidy, it would simply mean that the products of the west would be transported down to North Bay and out through American channels to American seaports. I did not conceive it to be within the line of my duty to support such a measure. The Bill was subsequently amended so that its eastern terminus would be at Quebec. That was a little better ; but I felt that even with that amendment, I should oppose the meas-Mr. EMMERSON.
urd, and I did. I realized that if the products of the west were brought to the east by that company as far as Quebec, perhaps during the summer months shipments would be made from the port of Quebec, but during the winter months every pound of traffic would go via Portland or Boston or some other American port, particularly Portland ; and I felt that that would be in the interest of the company. I realized that it would not be in their interest to transfer their freight at Quebec to the Intercolonial Railway. I realized that if you wished to make that company interested in utilizing Canadian winter ports, you must compel them to operate a road into the maritime provinces with the view of utilizing a port there ; and I did propose as an alternative that rather than build a railway aided by government funds from the Pacific to Quebec, to be treated in the way I have stated, it would be preferable for the government of Canada to extend the Intercolonial into the wheat fields of the west, where it could gather up the grain and bring it down to be shipped from Canadian ports during the winter months, even though it might be done at a loss. I argued that it would be better to do that than to give this proposed company the opportunity of taking the produce out by way of Portland. It is said that I am inconsistent in that respect. Why, Sir, I went further in that connection. When even the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) and other hon. gentlemen opposite in the committee were sneering at the proposition and scouting the idea that the Intercolonial would be extended into the west, I went further. I said : If you are opposed to extending the government line into the wheat fields of the west, construct a line into the west and give to some company the right to operate it ; place upon that company the onus of operating the road, and give rights over it to all companies which gather the wheat of the west into the great city of Winnipeg. At that time the government had not made its proposals.. At that time there was nothing in the air ; there were no whispers as to what should be done. It has been said that the suggestions which I made with respect to the extension of the Intercolonial into the wheat fields of the west were inspired by the then Minister of Railways. Let me say, in justice to that gentleman, that from the very beginning down to the close he did not consult with me nor confer with me in any way with respect to any policy in relation to the building of the transcontinental line; and when I made the suggestions which I did before the Railway Committee, I did it without any knowledge, other than what other hon. members had. as to the views of the then Minister of Railways and Canals. One thing I never did propose was a government-owned and operated road from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I did propose a gflxer nment-owned

and operated road to the wheat fields of the west; or as an alternative to that, a government-constructed and government-owned, but -eempany-operated road to the wheat fields of the west. Opposition to government ownership and government operation was so strongly in evidence in that committee that I realized the utter futility of any attempt being made to have an extension of the government railway into the west. There were very few who had any sympathy with the idea. I do not know of one hon. member sitting on the other side of the House who favoured the proposition in any degree. If the company has its terminus at a Canadian seaport in the east, there is no doubt that it wilj be to its interest to use it. That is the history of all railways. It is particularly the history of the Canadian Pacific Railway with respect to the city of St. John. When the Canadian Pacific Railway Company first got their short line railway it was with no idea that there would be an export trade through the port of St. John ; and it was only after years of persistence on the part of the people of Canada and the people of the maritime provinces, that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company made any movement towards the carrying out of that idea. Efforts were put forth by the people of St. John, the people of New Brunswick and the legislature of New Brunswick all urging that there should be an export trade. Even steamship lines were communicated with, negotiations were had, and it was by reason of the co-operation of the steamship lines with the government and with the Canadian Pacific Railway, that finally there was a start ; and it is only, I believe, since this government came into power that the full fruition of all that expenditure has been realized. Not the full fruition because the work is in progress. It is advancing year by year ; there are a great many strides in that direction, and the port of St. John is destined to become a great port for Canadian exports.
Subsequent to the understanding referred to in connection with the Railway Commission, the government announced its policy. True, it is not the original proposition as made by me, namely the extension of the Intercolonial to the western wheat fields, but it was at least the carrying out of an idea which I had foreshadowed in that committee in connection with the construction and ownership and operation of the line. The proposition in a few words is this : The .government should construct and own the road from Winnipeg 'to' the 'Maritime provinces via Quebec, and this road should be operated by the Grand Trunk Pacific, but should be open to all companies gathering wheat in the west wishing to have running rights over it. I know that it is certainly popular throughout New Brunswick. I realize that there is a strong feeling among the people there in favour of this proposition, and they are only hop-116}
ing that there shall be no more obstruction on the part of the opposition to delay the carrying out of this scheme. The proposal is certainly all that I would ask for and really more, because it insures the construction and ownership by the government, involving the control of rates and-the obviation Qf_aIJU-tiH^-TTPiycTr5ns which were so Ttften made by hon. gentlemen opposite to the operation of a railway by the government. What is of more importance perhaps, it is the shortest possible line from thq^ wheat centres of the west to the Atlantic sea-board, and that, considering our geo- ,f graphical position, is an element worthy of the greatest consideration. There is one thing lost sight of, it seems to me, in this discussion. We speak of this railway as one intended for the sole purpose of emptying the rich fields of the west out on the Atlantic sea-board, but to my mind it is equally for the benefit of the east and will provide a market for the products of the east. It will not merely provide a market for the manufacturers of Montreal and Toronto and other great centres in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, but also for the business men of the extreme east. To-day I know of one concern, which has been in existence in Moncton a number of years, a very prosperous manufacturing company, which is making every arrangement for taking advantage of the markets of the west and is hoping for a speedy consummation of this project.
I do not wish to repeat what has been so very eloquently expressed by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, but'I cannot refrain from making a reference to what we heard so much about last year, the proposition of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, known as the alternative proposition. That withering plant, which has never been watered by the favourable consideration of this House or even of the hon. gentleman's friends around him, or stimulated by the nourishing sunshine of popular approval, is entirely neglected this year. We do not hear of it at all. It is true that the faltering hesitancy regarding government ownership which was so much in evidence heretofore has been measurably removed, and we now have a northwest and east policy of government ownership. Some of the leaders on the other side say that the road should end at North Bay. Some say that it should not be built at all, and others pretend that we should purchase the Canada Atlantic and utilize the waterways. Let me say once and for all that individually I look upon any scheme that will extend the Intercolonial to Ontario with favour, and if the purchase of the Canada Atlantic would tend to that end I as an individual member, would favour that proposition. But the Transcontinental Railway scheme now under consideration is in no sense a bar to the carrying out of what is called the Georgian bay scheme. But I

a good deal of the evidence on this point has been cited by the Minister of Finance, there are some features and some facts, as taken from that paper, to which he has not referred. The ' Sun ' says, speaking of the purchase of the Canada Atlantic :
Again, it may be said that the purchase of the Canadian Atlantic, recommended by Colonel Tucker, would bring the Intercolonial Railway to Parry Sound, which is not exactly on any direct land route to the Pacific, though it is an important traffic line between the Intercolonial system and the great lakes. Finally, it will be noticed that Quebec and other places interested in the Trans-Canada route w'ould not find their purchase in the least disturbed by government extension from Montreal toward Georgian bay. What they want most is the development of that spacious portion of Quebec and province lying between Chicoutimi and James bay, a region supposed to have great possibilities. The demand for a railway through that country will still be pressed, no matter what government roads and Grand Trunk roads are built elsewhere. If the country is as rich as it is represented, and if the route is no longer and no harder than its advocates maintain, the claim cannot be resisted.
On May 14th, the St. John ' Sun,' referring to the question of the Grand Trunk Pacific in an editorial, contained the following :
The strong resolutions sent from the different legislatures, municipal and commercial bodies in the east are clear and explicit. They ask, one and all, that the Grand Trunk Pacific shall get no public assistance unless the company shall build to the maritime provinces and make a terminus at a maritime port. The boards of trade and other bodies know that an undertaking to deliver freight to the Intercolonial Railway is no good for the purpose they have in view'. From Quebec by the Intercolonial Railway is 111 miles farther than from Quebec to St. John by the circuitous route of the Intercolonial Railway. Temiseouata and the Canadian Pacific. The Grand Trunk extension from Quebec to St. John by the St. John valley would give a still greater advantage over the north shore route. But it is not worth while even to argue the case. The Grand Trunk people, the Intercolonial people, and the winter port people all know that export and import trade between the Canadian west and Europe can never be handled by the Intercolonial Railway route. We have had the test of six years' experience for one thing. Mr. Blair thought six years ago that he could do this business. He said so over and over again. He found that he was mistaken.
Again, in referring to tlie telegram of Mr. Blair to Mr. Jarvis, it says :
In view of these circumstances the reply of Mr. Blair to Mr. Jarvis is altogether unsatisfactory. Mr. Blair and Mr. Hays practically say the same thing. The Grand Trunk manager said a week ago that his company would be willing either to hand over to the Intercolonial Railway all the w'inter traffic that road could take or else to build to the coast. Mr. Blair wires to Mr. Jarvis :
' I believe that in case government gives financial assistance the Grand Trunk Pacific will be obliged either to enter into a satisfac-Mr. EMMERSON.
tory traffic agreement binding itself to hand over at Quebec its ocean winter traffic to Intercolonial Railtvay or build a line through to a maritime port. Have been doing everything possible to bring this about.
Now, here, to my mind, is the richest portion of this editorial:
The minister must have noticed that the resolutions and telegrams sent him do not ask this alternative.
There was no alternative proposition in their minds. It was not to he if the Intercolonial Bailway would not make satisfactory arrangements that this shorter line would be ibuilt into the maritime provinces, but it was that no matter what the Intercolonial Railway might do the shorter line would be built direct from Quebec into the maritime provinces.
The people of the maritime provinces, and, we believe, the people of Canada, do not propose to compromise on a traffic agreement with a road that cannot profitably handle the traffic. They insist on one thing and one only. They say that the Grand Trunk Railway itself must be built to a Canadian winter port. That is the message of Mr. Jarvis and the St. John Board of Trade. That is the resolution of the city council and the county council of St. John, of the legislature of New Brunswick, and of the other bodies which have made declarations on the subject.
These quotations from the [DOT] ' Sun ' suggest the attitude of Mr. Blair on this question and if I may be pardoned I will make some reference to that attitude. What was it ? It certainly is pertinent to notice what Mr. Blair's advice to his colleagues on that question was. We have heard what he saidi to the St. John Board of Trade. WTe have heard what he said to Mr. Jarvis. We have heard what his attitude ttns in the Railway Committee. Now, we refer to that celebrated confidential document, a document that was made famous by the fact that it was purloined and then introduced into the debate by the hon. leader of the opposition thereby taking away its confidential character. We learn from that what Mr. Blair regarded as the ideal railway policy. At the close of his memorandum of the 10th December, 1903, Mr. Blair said :
The ideal policy, as it appears to the undersigned, for the government to adopt, so soon as it shall be deemed necessary to take up the subject of a third transcontinenal railway, would be to insure, first, that the railway shall be wholly Canadian. That it shall not promote the carriage of our export products, or our imports southerly by way of United States lines of railway ; but to and from the St. Lawrence in summer and the ports of Halifax and St. John in winter. That the Quebec bridge be utilized as a part of said line, and that the railway be pushed westerly from that point by degrees to the Peace river district, through the Rockies to the Pacific coast. In the meantime, it would be well to decline all assistance to railways to which government is not already

committed, and propose to parliament that railway charters covering this territory be withheld.
Such a policy as that above outlined, the undersigned believes would meet the hearty support of the Canadian people, would materially strengthen the government, and would be regarded as both bold and progressive. The country is prepared to-day, as it has never been before, to assume large responsibilities in order to insure its fuller development, and government, if it fails to act, will lose a splendid opportunity of proving its capacity and courage to cope with and solve large problems in a manner commensurate with Canada's marvellous progress.
The essential features of what Mr. Blair calls the ideal policy have been adopted in the measure which was brought before parliament by the right hon. gentleman who leads the government. Now, the principal change is in respect to the Quebec-Moncton section. I am not going to argue in respect to that. My views were stated at some length last year in connection with the Quebec-Moncton section. I could, if time permitted, read the evidence of prominent lumbermen in the province of New Brunswick as to the importance from the local standpoint of developing and opening up the immense areas of rich timber and agricultural and hardwood forests which exist there. I shall not take up the time of the House by referring to these letters but the evidence is voluminous and it is at hand if any hon. members of the House wish to refer to it. But it is obvious that Mr. Blair, outside of the exception of the Quebec-Moncton section, as respects the remaining portion, the portion from Quebec to the Pacific coast which he apparently accepted, wanted the government to proceed at once declaring that if they hesitated they would not show their ability or courage to cope with great difficulties and he felt that the time was ripe for action. He wanted to stop all assistance to1 railways within the territory indicated. He declared that:
The country is prepared to-day, as it has never been before, to assume large responsibilities in order to ensure its fuller development.
And he goes on further and says :
And government, if it fails to act, will lose a splendid opportunity of proving its capacity and courage to cope with and solve large problems in a manner commensurate with Canada's marvellous progress.
It is said that this railway will cost a lot of money. Railways do cost money. They cannot be built without money and I am sure that if a comparison were made as to the estimated cost of this road with the proposal put forth by hon. gentlemen opposite there is certainly going to be a very great saving to the country by reason of the adoption of the government proposal. But, the very moment you admit that the work is necessary you admit the element of cost. Of course, we have this on authority
which has not been questioned, and which will not be questioned by hon. gentlemen opposite, namely, the authority of Mr. Blair :
The country is prepared to-day, as it has never been before, to assume large responsibilities in order to ensure its fuller development.	.
No one, of course, knows exactly what the precise cost will be, but it is safe to assume that it will not be one dollar more than is absolutely necessary. Can the opposition say that their scheme for a transcontinental railway will cost any less than that which has been proposed by the government ? Since no one denies that another railway spanning the continent is absolutely and imperatively necessary, let us see what it will accomplish. First, it will afford an outlet for the rapidly growing products of the great west; secondly, it will create needed competition in the transportation of merchandise to as well as from the west; thirdly, it will open up vast areas to settlement over the entire line ; fourthly, it will create a new source of wealth to the Dominion ; fifthly, it will allay the persistent irritation in the west over the transportation problem ; sixthly, it will demonstrate to. the world the enterprise and financial strength of the Canadian people.
I am sure that this last is a matter of very great importance to the people of this Dominion, because we wish to be recognized abroad as a country young it is true, but strong in our youth. We wish to let the world know that we have resources, and that we have both the courage and the ability to advance. I say boldly, that this measure has the approval of the country at large, it is popular in the west; it is popular in the east! Now, Mr. Speaker, I have *perhaps taken up more time than I had intended, and let me say in conclusion, that I have not changed my views one whit on this subject. As they were last year so are they this year. I believe that this scheme is one of the best that could be propounded in the interests of Canada, because it means a minimum of expense with a maximum of advantage to the people of this country. The proposition appeals to me even more strongly than it did last year as being in the highest interest of all Canada, and its consummation will be an epoch in the history of our land to which we may all look forward with the happiest expectations. It will make the beginning of national greatness for us. Let us trust that in the future the great author of this scheme will have the satisfaction of knowing that he built wisely and well for the future of Canada, and if perchance some day a great artist will arise to paint an allegorical picture descriptive of the right hon. gentleman leading the hosts of Canada up the steep declivity of national greatness, the right hon. Prime Minister will be represented carrying

a banner on which will be inscribed ' Canada's development and victory while in the valley below will be seen the Lilliputian figures of lion, gentlemen opposite who have tried and tried in vapi to obstruct the passage of this great national measure.

Mr. Blair then went on to say :
I fail to discover wherein we have to appeal to heaven against the possibility of a little delay in this matter. I know of no reason why the interests of Canada are going to be prejudicially affected because when we move forward we see the end, or think we see the end, to which we are looking, because we know the limits of the responsibility by which we assume to be bound, and because we believe we understand the conditions under which we are operating. Why is it said by my hon. friend, in this manner and in these terms, that we must not pause a moment to deliberate ?
I could quote at a great deal of length from the speech of the ex-Minister of Railways, but I shall content myself with quoting one more passage : I
I have studied the question somewhat, and I do not know just how soon or how far in the future the time might be when such a line as this would be called for by the west ; but now or in the immediate future there would have been no demand for any such railway project as this.
So that the charge made by the Minister of Finance that the opposition have changed their minds on this subject, that they did not believe there was any urgent necessity for such a road, and are now impressed with the fact that there is a great deal of Mr. BELL.
urgency for it, is absolutely lacking in foundation. That opinion was not expressed on this side, but was expressed and held so strongly by the ex-Minister of Railways that rather than join with his leader in carrying out the work we are now discussing, he preferred to resign his position and practically go into opposition to the measure. Although the speech of my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance, I must admit, was very clever from his standpoint, it had this defect that from first to last it did not meet any of the arguments or objections made from this side. He left those entirely aside and set himself to proving something which nobody disputes and to argue against contentions nobody has made. But he ignored completely all the strong points made against the contract from this side. For instance, we on this side hold that, in so far as any contract exists to compel the Grand Trunk Pacific to carry freight to Canadian ports, there is no guaranty at all. What does the Minister of Finance say in reply to that ? He simply read the clauses of the contract made, not with the Grand Trunk Railway, but the Grand Trunk Pacific, and asserts that these are not only more binding, comprehensive and definite than any proposition suggested from this side, but that they are actually all powerful, satisfactory and convincing and will compel the fulfilment by the Grand Trunk Pacific of all the contracts they have made. That is simply avoiding the whole issue and begging the question. What this side has contended is that the government has entered into a contract with what is really a dummy or a bogus company, if I may use the expression, a company called the Grand Trunk Pacific which was really set up to stand between the government and the Grand Trunk Railway and prevent the latter from incurring liability. What did the Minister of Finance say with reference to that point ? He simply passed it by. He refers to the letter of the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific and says that it is perfectly satisfactory, but the whole point of the argument on this side is that the Grand Trunk Railway is really the contracting company and should be called upon to bind itself to carry out this contract. Again he deals in the most ingenious fashion with the argument which he purports to derive from the report of the meeting of the Grand Trunk shareholders. He takes up the argument made by Mr. Allen, who, he says, was perfectly aware of the objections to the contract from the Grand Trunk point of view, and he assumes that Mr. Allen knew al'l the conditions and advantages of the amending contract. He argues that because the memo, of Mr. Allen was presented to the meeting of shareholders at the time the amended contract had been entered into and was submitted to the shareholders, he was in possession of the facts and that the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway were aware of all the

advantages in connection with the amended contract.
He ignores, in fact refuses to read, the statement in which the president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company says that Mr. Allen's language can only be accounted for by the fact that he is not acquainted with the provisions of the amended contract. And so from beginning to end, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has skated over every piece of thin ice in the bourse of his argument, and, in the end he has not added a single argument to the reasons that the government ought to be in a position to advance to induce the people to support the government measure. He winds up with the assertion, as did the Minister of Railways (Mr. Emmerson), that the country is wild for this contract; that in British Columbia every man is in fa you'1 of it, that in Ontario every man is in favour of it, that in New Brunswick every man is in favour of it, that in Nova Scotia every one-

That is what they would have us believe. This is no argument in favour of the Bill. It is a very good assertion for the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to have his colleagues make to keep up the courage of his followers. We are told that there is no better way of keeping up one's courage than by whistling, and in this case these hon. gentlemen are simply whistling to keep their courage up. They are evidently much afraid of the position in which they find themselves. Looking closely to the speech of the Finance Minister it is evident that the point he is afraid of and the point that the leader of the government is afraid of, is government ownership. And how does the Minister of Finance deal with it ? He tells us in the early part of his speech that he is going to take issue with the leader of the opposition fairly and squarely, that the government will meet the opposition in the country and prove to the people that government ownership is not a good thing for this country, and will challenge the opposition tc- make out a case. And then he proceeds to make out a case against government ownership. In order to do so he cites an opinion of the late Sir John A. Macdonald, also an opinion of the respected ex-leader of the Conservative party Sir Charles Tupper, adverse to government ownership ; and, apparently, he believes that he has convinced us, or should have convinced us, that, as these wise and great and eminent Conservative gentlemen expressed themselves in opposition to government ownership, therefore, government ownership is a thing that we should not support. It is good to learn that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has come to that state of mind to that improvement of judgment, in which the words of the late Sir John A. Macdonald have a
great deal of weight with him, in which he is ready to listen to Sir Charles Tupper as one who speaks with oracular truth and power. Of course, to the gentlemen on this side of the House, the opinions of these great statesmen, men who in the past have led them with success, with credit to them and benefit to the country, have a great deal of weight. But these leaders have passed from the scenes. The questions we are dealing with to-day are not those with which they dealt. And, while we look back with a great deal of reverence to their record in active politics, and will, unquestionably pay great attention to the deliberate opinion of such men, we know very well that, at this time, we must take the position that thd right hon. leader of the House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) said he was going to take. The time has come when we must decide. We cannot wait ; we cannot go back twenty years and accept the opinions, given, perhaps, correctly, by gentlemen of great knowledge in view of the circumstances that surrounded them. We have to deal with the situation as we find it to-day, and it is one in which we would have been glad to luar from the Finance Minister, had he had it to offer, sound argument against the principle of government ownership. What did the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) give in addition to the opinion of these great and eminent men 1 The final argument was that, whereas the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) at one time had expressed himself as having an opinion adverse to government ownership, therefore,- and this was the concluding argument, if I may dignify the remark with such a name -the leader of the opposition should take the advice of his railway expert and vote against government ownership. Well, it's a poor rule that won't work both ways. I would commend the advice of the Minister of Finance to the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and would suggest the advisability of his following the advice of his railway expert the present Minister of Railways and Canals, (Mr. Emmerson) who has expressed himself very strongly in favour of the principle of government ownership, and decide to abandon his Bill and vote for the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition. If it is a good rule for the leader of the opposition to be guided by his railway expert and decide these questions in that fashion, it must be a still better rule for the leader of the government to follow the advice of his railway expert, whom he had the opportunity of choosing himself, and in placing whom in his present office, no doubt he considered his fitness for the position. I do not know that the Finance Minister, in the course of the very long speech he made, dealt in anything like an argumentative sense with any other matter than this one. He led up to this one deliberately, announced that he was going to

know very well that the right hon. gentleman's answer to every one who says that the eastern division of this road may not pay is : We are not responsible ; the Grand Trunk Railway takes the burden off our shoulders. The Grand Trunk Railway Company stands between us and any possible loss, as far as the eastern part of the road is concerned. That would be satisfactory to the people of the country if it could be shown that the Grand Trunk was a corporation that ever sustained any burden or stress. What is the history of the Grand Trunk Railway Company ? It has already received S15.000.000 from the people of Canada, and it has never paid a cent of principal or interest. The Grand Trunk Railway Company is only earning about $800 a mile, and there is going to be a liability of $1,200 per mile on the eastern portion of this road, providing the whole costs $40,000 a mile. The right hon. leader of the government says that the people of Canada incur no liability, because the Grand Trunk Railway Company are going to take the liability off our shoulders. What is the strength of the Grand Trunk Railway Company as compared with that of the country ? The fact of the matter is that the moment a difficulty arises which compels the Grand Trunk Railway Company to go into default, it will throw up its hands, and the responsibility falls back upon the government. What has been the experience during the past year ? The right hon. gentleman last year brought before this House a contract which could not be touched in any particular, because it had been made with the company and had to be observed by this country and by the government. We could not affect it. The most necessary and legitimate amendments had to be voted down, because embodied in that Bill was a contract which was sacred, and the most powerful inducements to amend that contract could not be listened to for that reason. The Bill having become law, what was the result ? What the company had contracted to do in respect of the deposit of $5,000,000 it did not litid it convenient to do. Did the company sweat, or worry, or fret about it ? The company simply went into default. The result was that the right hon. gentleman and his government were practically taken by the throat and were compelled to make such amendments as the company required. There is no doubt about the accuracy of that statement. Proof of it is to be found in the speech in which the right hon. leader of the government introduced the amendments this year, and in that portion of the speech of the hon. Finance Minister to-night in which he dealt with the amendments. As far as the hon. gentlemen who have dealt with these amendments are concerned, they have simply recited them, stated their meaning and why they yield this, why they yield that and why they yield the other. They did not "want very much. They wanted only one Mr. BELL.
sleeve of our coat, then they wanted the other sleeve, then they wanted the skirt, and the result was that they took the whole coat. Apparently, judging from the speech of the right hon. leader of the government and the hon. Minister of Finance, the government were utterly helpless. They had their project, the success of which project was bound up in getting the Grand Trunk Railway Company to go on with it. The Grand Trunk Railway Company said : We cannot do it, because the money market is not favourable. We cannot make our deposit ; and down came the government. The government yielded, and we may fairly suppose that the government will yield again before another year passes. If the company find out that all that is necessary, in order to get better-terms, is to refuse to go on they will not fail to profit by that lesson ; yet in place of accepting the proposition made by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition that the .Country, paying pine-tenths of the cost, should own and operate the road, the right hon. gentleman seems determined at any cost to hold on to the company. The extraordinary hold the company have upon this government is shown by a rather singular occurrence that took place here this evening. I do not know that a more extraordinary thing was ever known to take place in a British parliament than that a gentleman occupying the position of Minister of Finance should have allowed weeks and months to pass before he ventured to give to this House which was engaged in discussing this measure, an authoritative statement of the financial aspect of this measure, and of what the cost of the road would be.
The Minister of Finance comes here at the eleventh hour and the fifty-ninth minute when it is impossible to test the accuracy of his figures, and he gives to the House information that should have been given the very day the Bill was first introduced. In addition to that, the ,Minister of Finance has the distinction of having tabled to-night the demand made upon the government by the Grand Trunk Railway Company for assistance for the construction of their road through the west. Now, we know what we should have known long ago ; that the demand was for $6,400 and 5,000 acres of land per mile. And in this connection we were told that the government of Canada had actually to get the permission of Mr. Hays to inform the parliament of Canada of the demand that was made upon the people of Canada by that corporation. Sir, such a thing is degrading both for the government and for the country. Imagine the government of Canada asking permission of Mr. Hays to reveal to the representatives of the sovereign power of the people of this country, a matter affecting the interests of the people. No more extraordinary thing has even taken place in any parliament. There was something

about the speech of the Finance Minister which afforded me great gratification. 1 used to know the hon. gentleman in Nova Scotia. I sometimes had very serious regrets about his course of conduct, but tonight when I learned what an intensely loyal and patriotic man he has become, I felt that I was rewarded for all I had suffered from him in the past, and furthermore for all the good advice I have given him. A few years ago the Minister of Finance was premier of Nova Scotia, and he was then an ardent repealer who could not think anything or say anything good of Canada, and whose mission in this world was to carry his province out of this frightful confederation. He is the gentleman who once said : that the idea that the Canadian Pacific Railway should be built, before a road was built in Prince Edward Island, was absurd. At that time the Minister of Finance was so provincial and so lacking in national sentiment, and so disloyal to our institutions, that I was delighted to hear him confess to-night that whether we had a good country or a bad country : ' this is our country.' I am pleased to find that the Minister of Finance with such a record in the past, is in a position to-night to take to his breast the whole of this country ; its jack pine, its muskegs and its granite ridges. I have never seen in my public career any sign to give me so much satisfaction, and I can hope that the conversion shall be a lasting one. It took a long time to come, but under able tuition and with good example, and with the inspiring reward of high office and some emolument, in the greater and larger sphere my friend has gotten over these little delinquencies of his, and has rid himself of that desire for flirtation with secession and repeal. While my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is litre to-night to admire everything that is Canadian and to talk as a solid Canadian, you cannot imagine what pleasure it gives me when I reflect, that he is the same gentleman who a few years ago writing for the instruction of the people of Nova Scotia, addressed them in this language :
If you do this the battle will he fought and won, the enemy dethroned and Nova Scotia set free to enter upon that career of usefulness and success which nature ever intended should b? hers, and hers alone.
People of Nova Scotia, if you have any of that latent fire and enthusiasm which once throbbed in your hearts, and in the hearts of your fathers, let it be awakened and aroused ; let the principles of justice and liberty, the love of freedom and of home once more animate and inspire you ; let your dearest rights, privileges and institutions be nobly espoused and gallantly upheld ; let the vials of your righteous indignation be poured forth against those who would further bind you by that monstrosity of legislation-the British North America Act- and let it be said to-day that you have championed the cause of political freedom, that you have thrown off the Canadian monster, and
emancipated yourselves and your beloved province from the thraldom, the servitude and the bondage of the Canadian union !
I do not know that I ever in my life enjoyed such a feeling of satisfaction and delight as when to-night I heard the Minister of! Finance use the language that a Canadian statesman should use. He is no longer tainted with this dislike of the British North America Act. No longer does he hate his brother Canadians ; no longer does he indulge in petty provincialism ; no longer does he insist on having railways built in Prince Edward Island, before railways are built in the west; he is to-day ready to build a railway through jackpines, western muskegs and granite ridges. We cannot allow the right hon. gentleman to forget that he it was that first introduced the muskeg and the jackpine in this discussion. I do not know whether the right hon. gentleman knew a jackpine from a muskqg, but I am disposed to think that he referred to these things innocently, not knowing what damage his reference might do to the fair name of our country. However, I must repel the insinuation that the jackpine and the muskeg originated on this side of the House. We are perfectly prepared to accept our friends on the other side of the House as being loyal to-day, but we do not like a certain effort that is all the time being made to try to force the opposition in this House into the position of belittling the country. We do not belittle or decry the country throughout which this railway may run. We are perfectly satisfied to say that we do not know anything about it, but we hope the best for it. What is the argument of the Finance Minister in that connection? He has apparently made up his mind to love it all, good or bad, because it is our country. But when you come to deal with commercial matters, sentiment is not the only thing that is to be considered. A country that is well governed would not build a railway into an unproductive district simply because, in the words of the Finance Minister, it is our country. If we were going to occupy our country fully, we would have to gridiron the whole north with rails, and that is not what any rational government would recommend.
There is one feature of this discussion in which the Finance Minister took a certain amount of interest and pleasure ; that was in developing the idea that there is a tremendous desire for this particular road in the maritime provinces, and therefore no maritime province man could safely oppose it. I should not think that was proper teaching for the Finance Minister to give to any representative body. It is to my mind rather a provincial way of looking at the matter. In discussing a railway which is to span the continent, we should not consider exactly how it is going to impress every polling section in the country. If it is a

good scheme, it may be necessary for a man to take the unpopular course of supporting it-unpopular so far as his constituency may he concerned. If it is a wrong scheme, it may be the duty of a public man to oppose it and thereby incur a great deal of odium. Each man must decide for himself what he will do. We should get rid of these small sectional views, and regard the measure from the standpoint of the nation, and express the truth about it even if that should cause a certain amount of loss of strength in particular localities. But to my mind there is no reason at all why the maritime provinces should be excited over this project. The Finance Minister was very careful to say that he did not know whether this project would succeed in carrying grain to the sea or not; and if the hon. gentleman who has the opportunities which he has to inquire into that matter is unable to satisfy himself on that point, surely we in the opposition may examine the measure critically and find out what defects are in it without incurring hostility on the part of our constituents. There is a way in which the government, if disposed to bring about the carrying of the grain traffic to the maritime province, could effect that result at once, without building any railway at all. They have only to take the amount of money required to meet the interest on the outlay on the eastern portion of this road, and devote it to bonusing the carriage of wheat from the west to the east over the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway and over the Intercolonial from Montreal, in order to divert a large amount of that traffic at once, without losing time in waiting for a railway to be built. The Intercolonial last winter carried freight at the rate of 9-100 cent per ton per mile ; and at that rate it is quite possible to carry to Halifax and St. John a large portion of the grain traffic of the west, and realize at once for those ports the benefits of being the winter ports through which the grain will flow. But under the scheme now proposed, if you are going to exact such rates as the Grand Trunk manager, Mr. Wainwright, said before a commission of this House were absolutely essential in order to yield earnings, you are not going to see any important part of the grain traffic of the west carried directly to the ports of the maritime provinces.
There is not to my mind any case made out against the arguments of the opposition. All the points that have been made in reference to the common stock, in reference to the propriety of more stringent control over the action of the Grand Trunk, in reference to the necessity of controlling the arrangement made between the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific, are all strong arguments against the present scheme, and not one of them has been met by hon. gentlemen on the government side of the House. The Finance Minister, Mr. BELL.
in speaking of the common stock, speaks as if the concession made to the company at the present time is a very trifling one. Last year he referred to the provision which prevented the common stock being sold to the Grand Trunk Company as one of the utmost importance. What is the effect of the Grand Trunk Company holding the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company ? There is $25,000,000 of common stock, and $20,000,000 of preferred stock which represents the voting power of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company ; and so long as the $23,000,000 of stock is in the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, so long will that company constitute the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, and it will to a certain extent be responsible for the operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific. But now that the government has consented to allow the Grand Trunk Company to dispose of that stock, that security for which the Finance Minister held out last year, is lost I would have liked him to have dealt more fully with that subject, and to have explained to what extent he believed that not only the common stock but the preferred stock should have voting power and should be held by the Grand Trunk Company. Although this matter has not been discussed previously in this debate, it strikes me as singular that so little has been said as to the disposition to be made of the preferred stock.
I would have liked very much if the Minister of Finance had dealt more particularly with that subject, but he did not see fit to do so. But so far as the releasing of the Grand Trunk Railway from the obligation to hold $25,000,000 of the stock is concerned, it simply amounts to this, that the Grand Trunk Railway is in effect the Grand Trunk Pacific and yet is in a position to sell the stock and place it upon the market and get out of any obligation whatever that might otherwise rest upon it. The Bill has been discussed at very great length by the opposition, and has been shown to possess serious defects. I regret very much that the government have not been able to bring arguments to meet the objections from this side. I particularly regret that at no time in the course of this discussion has anything like adequate consideration been given to the sti'ong point made by the leader of the opposition to the effect that whereas the government is practically contributing nine-tenths of the cost of the road and assuming all the liability, it ought to contribute the other tenth and own and operate the whole road in the interests of the people.

Before the main motion is carried, I beg to move :
That the Bill be not now read the third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole with instructions to amend the same by adding the following as section No. :
Notwithstanding anything in this A<?t or in the supplementary agreement contained the government shall have and may exercise all rights, powers and remedies in respect of possession, foreclosure and sale upon default by the Pacific Company in the payment of interest on the bonds guaranteed by the government as. fully and effectually to all intents and purposes as if the sixth, seventh and eighth clauses of the said supplementary agreement were not therein contained, and as if the said three clauses formed no part of the scheduled agreements, or of any agreement between the parties thereto.
I do not intend to make any lengthened remarks on this subject. When the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) was making his speech a short time ago he was a little factious about the leader of the opposition not having me as the seconder of his motion. Nothing would have afforded me greater pleasure than to second that motion, but as I moved this resolution when in Committee of the Whole I would have been debarred



from moving it if I had seconded the motion of my hon. leader. I suppose the Finance Minister is satisfied after the remarks I made in support of the resolution of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition tfiat 1 would have no objection to seconding that motion. I have nothing further to add at this late hour to the arguments I used in committee in support of my present amendment. The government are incurring a larger financial responsibility than was originally intended. I see the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) in his place. I wonder what he will have to tel) us about the proposition he made-the Finance Minister did not mention it in his financial statement [DOT] that he was going to set aside a quantity of land in the Northwest from the sale of which the government would be enabled to meet part if not the whole of the expenditure tfiat they will be put to in connection with this scheme of the Grand Trunk Pacific.
