speechtext: I altogether agree with my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden), I must ask hon. gentlemen on this side to keep better order.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: It is quite unnecessary that any additional argument should be advanced to convince the House and the country of the necessity of pressing this prairie section of the road to a speedy finish.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
If the road is necessary at all the only part that is' immediately necessary is the prairie section. That section, as every one knows who is at all conversant with that country is easily constructed, compared with the eastern division or with the mountain section. There are no clearings to be effected until the road reaches whichever pass in the Rocky Mountains is to be taken-fellow-head, Pine or Peace River pass. Settlers are going in all through that country, so that I am satisfied that the amendment 1 have presented will meet with the hearty approval of the entire Northwest. I shall not attempt further to convince the Prime Minister. I had hoped in the early part of the session that he would withdraw the Bill. All we can hope now is that he will accept some of the amendments that we are offering to the measure.
Amendment (Mr. Sam. Hughes) negatived on the same division.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
I beg to move .
That the hill be not now read the third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole with instructions to amend the same by adding the following as section No.
Notwithstanding anything in this Act or in the Act hereby amended, or in the scheduled agreements contained, His Majesty the King acting as aforesaid, shall not be bound or obliged to perform, carry out or fulfil any of the covenants, conditions or stipulations in the said scheduled agreements contained on behalf of the Dominion of Canada, unless and until the Grand Trunk Company shall have entered into an agreement with His Majesty the King, acting as aforesaid, by which the said Grand Trunk Company shall covenant and agree as follows : That the Pacific Company, so long as the Grand Trunk Company shall control the policy of the company, shall perform, fulfil and carry out according to the true intent and meaning thereof, all the provisions of the National Transcontinental Railway Act and all the covenants, stipulations and agreements in the scheduled agreements, which according to the terms thereof ought to he performed, fulfilled or carried out by the said Pacific Company.
Having moved this amendment in Committee of the \\ hole, and having taken occasion then to express my views pretty fully upon the question, and considering the length of time that has been occupied-and, I think, well occupied-in the discussion of the measure before the House to-night, i would not, at this late hour, attempt to discuss the matter further or to add to what 1 have already said upon the question, except to urge upon the House one point in connection with this amendment.
There may be room for discussion and for a difference of opinion upon the amendments that have been offered to this Bill and upon the merits of the Bill itself, but the object of this resolution is that once the conditions and stipulations have been agreed upon between this government * and the Gnand

Trunk Pacific Railway there can be no further doubt as to what those conditions are, and having settled those conditions X conceive it to be the duty of this government or of any party to see that these covenants or conditions are carried out. That is the sole object of this resolution. The government has neglected this duty. I would not have said this much Mr. Speaker, as it must be apparent to every member of this House that it is only fair and in the interest of the country that the performance of the conditions of this contract should in some way be secured to the eountry. When I introduced this amendment in the committee, hon. members on the government side of the House saw fit to treat it with silence I can conceive of their adopting that course only from one of two reasons, either that members of the government considered that this amendment was unworthy of discussion, or they considered that the principle involved in this amendment was unanswerable. I cannot believe that members on the government side believed that the principle contained in this amendment was unworthy of discussion but I do believe, and I feel we have had every evidence of it during the discussion of this measure, that it is by reason of the manner in which individual opinion on the government benches has been stifled in this matter and the fear that the discussion of amendments such as I have introduced here will expose in a still greater degree than has already appeared, the weakness of the government upon this matter that they have chosen to treat the amendment with silence.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
Before the question is put, I would like to call the attention of the government to a matter of some moment, namely that on no less than four or five occasions during the present session and during the previous session members asked the government for copies of all correspondence and documents relating to the project which we have been discussing for the past few weeks. On page 447 of ' Hansard ' of last year it will be seen that the hon. member for St. Mary's division, Montreal (Mr. Tarte) moved for :
Copies of all correspondence between the government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company, or Mr. C. M. Hays, per William Wainwright, or any other person, In relation to a new transcontinental railway.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
I would ask my hon. friend not to press that motion at this stage of the session. Communications chiefly verbal have taken place between the government and the parties representing the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, hut no definite conclusions of any kind have been arrived at. Matters are still under discussion. So it would be quite impracticable for us to bring down any correspondence until a later stage, which we will be glad to do during the ' present session.
1174	.
Later on my bon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) asked a somewhat more comprehensive series of questions involving the same matters. One of the questions he asked was this :
Is it a fact that some members of the government are urging the said Grand Trunk Company to purchase the Mann & iftackenzic system ; and that the said Grand Trunk Company is asking for a large land grant, as a condition of said proposed purchase ?
To this the following answer was returned :
It'is not a fact that members of the government are urging the Grand Trunk Company to purchase the Mackenzie and Mann system, nor is the Grand Trunk Company asking for a large land grant as a condition for such a purpose.
Then another question asked by the hon. meber for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) was this :
Is it a fact that divisions in the cabinet are the sole cause of such delay ?
To this the answer was :
This is not a proper question, and if it were a proper question, the answer would be : There is not the slightest foujulation in fact for such a statement.
I am mentioning that for the purpose of showing that the attention of the government had been particularly directed to this question. Again, on April 2nd, the hon. member for Jacques Cartier put a further question to the government on the same subject and he received the answer from the government through the then Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Blair) the concluding portion of which is as follows :
But it would be premature to make any announcement now. As soon as this can be done in the public interest, parliament will be informed fully.
A further motion was made, to be found
in ' Hansard ' p. 1031, to which practically the same answer was returned. During the present session my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier moved for
Copies of all letters, telegrams, cables and memoranda exchanged between the government and the authorities of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, or the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, regarding the new transcontinental railway project, including the eastern division thereof.
He said : Mr. Speaker, before the motion is carried I would like to add to it the words ' since the last session of parliament.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Monk), before putting this amended motion, that I brought forward all we have upon this subject. Indeed there is nothing else.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: I have not seen the return. Does it purport to cover everything absolutely ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: If it does not I would press my motion because I ask for every communication of every nature whatever.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: I brought down everything upon the subject.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: My right hon. friend may understand that he may have deposited on the table of the House everything that he considered necessary or essential, but, this motion goes farther. Does my right hon. friend's report cover everything ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
I brought down everything without any equivocation at all, that we have on the subject.
Then again at page 590, replying to myself, the right hon. Prime Minister said :

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
I have to inform my hon. friend that everything relating to this matter has been laid before the House, the letter of the president of the company, Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson, making certain requests, and the concessions made by the government.
Then, further on I spoke on the Orders of the Day of April 20th, to this effect:
Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to ask the government whether there is or Is not any correspondence between the government and either the Grand Trunk Railway Company or the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company relating to the Transcontinental Railway project, wl#ch has not yet been brought down, and also whether there are any papers or documents relating to that project or negotiations with these companies, or either of them, which have not yet been brought down?
To which the right hon. gentleman replied as follows :
As to correspondence with either the Grand Trunk Pacific or Grand Trunk Railway Company, I have to inform my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) that there is no correspondence- everything has been brought down.
Now, to-night after these assurances have been given to the House and to the country on so many different occasions we have my hon. friend the Minister of Finance producing for the first time a document from the Grand Trunk Pacific Company to the government dated as far back as December, 1902, and presenting that for the first time to the House, after all these declarations have been made in parliament. I would like to know on what ground my hon. friends can justify that position. We have had these assurances from time to time that every document would be brought down during the past session and afterwards on two occasions at least that every thing had been brought down without any equivocation or evasion whatever, yet to-night the Minister of Finance reads to the House a public document upon' a public subject with regard to public aid demanded by the Grand Trunk Pacific for a public undertaking in this country. He reads that after we have all these declarations and assurance from the government that no such document existed. And strangest of all he thought he could not read it until the Grand Trunk gave him permission to read it to the parliament

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
and the people of ths country. You might as well call an Act of parliament confidential as to call that document confidential, a petition asking for public aid to a public undertaking in this country. The Minister of Finance who had not the courage to make his financial statement when it could be answered, sees fit to make it in the closing hours of the debate. We have that document introduced in the closing hours of the debate by permission of the Grand Trunk. It is fortunate that they were kind-hearted and generous enough to give that permission, otherwise we would not have known anything about it.
If it had not been that the government thought it was in their own interest at this iate moment to spring that document upon the parliament of this country after the repeated assurances which they had given that no such document existed we would have gone on accepting the assurance which they had given and we would have gone on believing that the right hon. leader of the government had stated the fact accurately to this House when he made the statement over and over again that every document had been brought down without evasion or equivocation. I do not understand on what principle the government trifles with parliament in this way. How is it that the right hon. gentleman ventured to say on more than one occasion, how is it that he ventured to say during last session through his Minister of Railways and Canals that every document would be brought down and how is it that he ventured to say only on the 20th April last that every document had been brought down without evasion or equivocation and how is it that the hon. Minister of Finance, to-night, by the kind permission of the Grand Trunk Railway Company brings down for the first time this public document to the parliament of this country? My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) spoke of the supposed necessity of obtaining the permission of the Grand Trunk Railway Company in strong terms but those strong terms should be made infinitely stronger when we consider the assurances and declarations that the government have given over and over again to parliament that every document on this subject has been brought down. I cannot understand it unless there has been some lapse of memory on the part of my right hon. friend, and I shall await with a great deal of interest the explanation which I think is due to the House from the right hon. gentleman on this subject.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will be a very easy matter to give my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) the explanation to which he thinks he is entitled as to what he imagines to be a laches on the part of the government in regard to this subject. I have to tell him

that I am not disposed at all in any way to accept the lecture which he has thought it advisable to give to me. If the hon. gentleman does not understand the reason why this document was not brought down it is simply because I, at all events-I do not know what his manner may be-when I receive a letter which is marked ' confidential ' do not think that I am authorized to bring it down to parliament. Every one has his own way of looking at these things If there are hon. gentlemen in this House who believe that when they receive a letter which is marked ' confidential ' they are not bound to keep it secret but that they have a right to bring it down and give it'to the public, I do not share their views. If Mr. Hays, or anybody else, approaches the government in a confidential manner his confidence must be respected. In this matter there were communications coming from the Grand Trunk Railway Company which were not marked ' confidential,' which were public and which were filed in the archives of the department and all these communications were brought down when they were asked for. Whether my views conflict or do not conflict with the views of hon. gentlemen opposite all I have to say is that for my part as long as I am here, whether I am addressed simply as an individual member or as the head of the government, by whomever it may be, let it be by one iii ever so humble a position or so high a position, if I am addressed in a confidential manner his confidence shall be respected. I want to know was there anything in that correspondence, which, if it had been brought down, could have been of any service to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House? Was there anything in it which could have helped them in the discussion ? Was there anything concealed in which the public could be interested in any way ? This confidential letter was in my own possession. This is the explanation which I have to give to my hon. friend. I did not think I was justified in bringing down that letter which was addressed to me and marked 1 confidential.' I could not give it to the public until I had written to Mr. Hays, asking him to allow me to give it to the public. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) said a moment ago that it was a degradation to ask the permission of Mr. Hays. All I have to say to my hon. friend is that my views differ from his upon this matter. It would have been a degradation to have betrayed the secret of anybody by bringing down to the public a letter which had been marked 'confidential.' If I had done that I would have been degraded in my own eyes and I would have had to accuse myself of having so far forgotten myself as to submit to the public a document which was marked 'private.' This correspondence lasted for a long time and when Mr. Hays gave us a communication which
we had to file in the archives of the department, it was brought down as I said last session, and I repeat again that every communication has been brought down without any evasion or equivocation whatever.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that parliament, tonight, is treated to a new divergence from the usual course.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: Certainly it is. The right hon. leader of the government speaks of confidential correspondence. A confidential petition to parliament praying for aid for a public undertaking

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: It was not to parliament.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
It was to the government in the first instance, but to the country in the main, and had the stipulation been carried out the country would have been obliged to have fulfilled the requirements of It. Now. this matter has two features that seem to require attention. One is the absolute assertion over and over again that everything had been brought down. There was no explanation that everything that was not confidential had been brought dowr. but the statement that everything had been brought down implied that whether or not confidential communications had passed everything had been presented to this House. The second is as to the courtesy with which parliament is treated. I have yet to learn that parliament and the country were not entitled to that information which the House got only to-night. Why did the House not get it last session? When it answered the purpose of the hon. Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) to give confidential communications to the House he gave them and when it answered the purpose of the government to give this confidential communication to the House it was brought down and not till then. There is no rule that will apply to one side of the House and that will not apply to the other side. If it was right to bring it down the House should have had it in the first instance and if it was right that it should be kept from the House, if it was of a confidential nature there is no justification to give it now. But, in my opinion it could not properly be considered as a confidential communication. The House should have been in possession of it to enable it to wisely and carefully consider the various propositions that were made to the country through parliament and had to come to a conclusion in reference to this matter.
If the rule holds good all that is necessary to the withholding of any of these communications is to mark them confidential, and if the government do not desire

370S
to give them to the House an intimation may he given to the parties with whom they are having communication to mark their communications ' confidential.' But, there is a better standard than that by which these things should be judged and it is that when any application is made for assistance from any source to this parliament, parliament is entitled to have that information given to it at the earliest possible moment, and it' has not treated parliament with the consideration with which the representatives of the people should be treated if such information is withheld from the House.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: I do not see how the Prime Minister can justify his conduct. The course he decided upon involved him in giving incorrect information to the House. The government was asked whether the company had applied for land grants, and the reply was that they had not; whereas the fact is brought out to-night by the Pnance Minister, that they had applied for 5,000 acres per mile, and yet through the mistaken course of the premier he is led to state to the House what is absolutely opposed to the fact. How could the Prime Minister have possibly stated to the House that the company had not asked for a land grant ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: That is quite easily explained.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: There is no propriety in allowing public documents of this kind to obtain a confidential character. They come to the ministers as a committee of this parliament, and to treat such communications as confidential is giving an advantage to the authors of them which they should not possess. If such documents are to be treated as confidential, even after negotiations have been concluded, it is laying down a principle that no House of Commons should ever assent to for all that any one would have to do is to mark a document sent to the government ' confidential,' and then it remains a secret from the representatives of the people in this parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: May I be permitted a personal explanation ? The letter which was brought down this afternoon by my hon. friend the Finance Minister, was addressed to me in November, 1902, and it was with reference to a project of the Grand Trunk to be assisted to build a railway from North Bay to the Pacific ocean

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: I understood the Minister of Finance to state that it was a petition for public aid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: It was a petition addressed to the government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: It was a petition addressed to the government for public aid.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: Sir WILFRID LAURIER, Personally it. w-as a letter to obtain assistance for a railway from North Bay to the Pacific ocean. This proposition was not entertained in any way whatever. Then the Grand Trunk Company made the other proposal which has been placed before the House, for the construction of a railway from Quebec to the Pacific ocean.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: Late as the hour is we should not allow this incident to pass without an earnest protest. I have not had long experience in parliament, but I can say that the answers given time and again by ministers to questions put by gentlemen on this side of the House, have not been as candid as they should be between gentlemen, not to speak of the fact that the information was givenn by ministers to representatives of the people. I would ask the Prime Minister, if we now have all the papers in possession of the government. If the right hon. gentleman says that he has now produced everything, am I to take his word, or, am I to suppose that there still may be something confidential which has not been produced? Is not that a most extraordinary position for a Prime Minister to place himself in ? The right hon. gentleman did not say he had produced everything except papers that were confidential, but he said ' without any equivocation,' to use his own words, that he had produced everything. The right hon. gentleman misled the House by saying that he had produced everything. Are we to understand in the future, that when a minister answers a Question in plain Eng-iish, we are to cross-examine him to ascertain whether there is something behind, so that we may know the true meaning of his reply ? We were told most distinctly that every document in the possession of the government had been produced-that was said without any reservation-and yet we have a most formal public document relating to the subject we have been discussing all last session and this, laid upon the Table at the last minute. That document was concealed from the representatives of the people in parliament.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance is very fond of cheap victories, and to-night he has unconsciously disclosed a conspiracy against the rights of the Canadian people. He read what he said was a petition. and that petition was an offer made by the Grand Trunk as against the Trans-Canada, and Mr. Hays very ingeniously consented that that document should be marked ' private ' in order that the government would have an excuse for withholding it. The right hon. gentleman has told us that he has a code of honour of his own. Has he the same code of honour as the Postmaster General who sits beside him, and who did not hesitate to publish broad-

cast, letters that were marked ' confidential.'
I know of no more serious thing than that the government should deliberately conceal documents that belong to the public.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: I hardly think that is parliamentary.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
What is it ?
Mr, SPE AKER. I do not think it is parliamentary for an lion, gentleman to say that there was a deliberate concealment.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: Perhaps I shall be warranted in saying deliberately withheld.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: I do not think that is any better.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: Well, I will withdraw that, and say that the Prime Minister unconsciously withheld it-that he was not acting upon his own will or motion, but was acting on the advice of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. X know of no more serious charge against the ministry than to say that documents that belong to the people have been withheld under any pretext whatever. These documents belong to the people the moment the negotiations proceed. Probably no incident in this whole affair reflects less credit on the government than this very transaction.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
As my right hon. friend does not quite agree with my recollection, I would like to say that the document begins as follows :
To the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, G.C.M.G., P.C., premier of the Dominion of Canada, Ottawa :
Your petitioners desire to memorialize your government in regard to the construction of a first-class line of railway from the northern terminus of the Grand Trunk Railway at or near North Bay, Ontario, through to the Pacific coast.
And it ends :
Your petitioners ask that your government will give the prayer of this petition their early and most earnest consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: There can be no question that if the government had taken any action on that petition with the view of bringing down to parliament a measure based thereon, then the idea of such a document being confidential could not be entertained, and it would have been the duty of the government to ask the authors of that document to remove the word ' confidential.'

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: Why was the document read ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: For good and sufficient reasons. But we are now dealing witn the question whether the government were bound to bring it down at an earlier stage. The government were not bound, first, because it was a confidential document.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says no, and yet he sees staring him in the face the word * confidential ' on the document.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: I say no document of this kind can be confidential.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: Any man who writes a letter to another man has a right to make it confidential. If the man who receives it has any reason to think that it should be made public he must apply to the author of the document and obtain his permission to make it public. In this case the document was not dealt with ; parliament was not asked to do anything in relation to that document ; and I dispute the contention of the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker), that in bringing down a return or in answering a question in this House a minister is bound to take notice of any documents that are confidential. Such documents must be ignored. The suggestion that we should say that we have a document, but it is confidential, is out of the question. If a document is confidential* it must be treated as such, and no reference whatever can be made to it. So much with regard to the non-production of the document earlier. The hon. member for Cornwall (Mr. Pringle) says, why bring it down now ? Not because it has any relation to the scheme before parliament, but because hon. gentlemen opposite in their efforts to discredit the scheme have made erroneous statements, and in order to correct those statements we have asked the author of the document to remove the seal of secrecy, so that we might bring it down.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman contend that it relates to the scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: I say it relates to statements made by hon. gentlemen in discussing the scheme, but not to the scheme itself. Hon. gentlemen opposite, in their endeavours to discredit the scheme, have made unfounded statements in reference to the Grand Trunk proposal. It is because of those statements and not because the document related to the merits of the scheme, that it was brought down, and it was proper that it should not be brought down without the consent of the gentlemen who wrote it.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: That document refers to the building of a transcontinental railway. Have we not been dealing exactly with the same question and with the same individuals, so that the document must have to do with the subject before the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: We have not been dealing with any scheme touched by that document whatever.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
1 interjected a remark to the right hon. the Prime Minister

over which he seemed to have got very touchy.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: I dare say that questions concerning fine points of honour are quite unknown to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, but we do not expect him to be a judge of these matters at all. In my opinion the duty of the First Minister, the moment he received a public document marked ' private and confidential,' was not even to read it, but to return it to Mr. Hays and the Grand Trunk Railway and notify them that no such document could be received subject to any such restriction, but could only be received as an official document. Just fancy a petition to the Prime Minister, to be handed to his government, being treated as a confidential document. It looks very much as if this matter had been borderiug on conspiracy for a long time before the people were taken into the confidence of the government. It looks as though a great many negotiations had been going on before anything was made public. Public documents should be treated as such, and the duty of the Prime Minister was to have returned this document unread, and notify the parties who sent it that it could not be acepted unless the words ' private and confidential ' were removed.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: In his speech this evening and afternoon, the hon. the Finance Minister said that myself with others had not dealt fairly with the government in our estimate of the cost of the construction of the road from North Bay westward. After the answer had been given by the right hon. the Prime Minister that all information, papers, and documents relating to this question had been laid on the Table, what other conditions could I assume than that the Grand Trunk Pacific had asked for the construction of this road on other basis than those which had been submitted to this House. We in the opposition should have the same information upon a subject of this character as the Prime Minister or any of his colleagues in the cabinet. We have a right to be given the fullest details. I believed that we were given the fullest information and was therefore warranted in stating that the Grand Trunk Railway had agreed to construct from North Bay westward for the ordinary subsidy granted to railway construction in this country. It is unfair that at the last moment the Finance Minister should bring forward a document, hitherto unknown to parliament, and base an argument on it. It was unfair and unjust. I know nothing of the rule of government and perhaps as little of the rules of parliament, but I know the rules of fair-play, and I say that it is only fair-play that the man who stands up and opposes a great governmental scheme should be put in possession of all information pertaining to it.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: Perhaps it might be well to go back some months and

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: inquire what effect the concealement of this petition had on the legislation in this House. I remember when the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill was introduced and referred to the Railway Committee, the hon. the Finance Minister was asked whether it was the intention of the Grand Trunk Pacific to ask for any assistance, and he said it was time enough to arrange the terms when the Grand Trunk Pacific did ask for assistance. On the strength of that misleading statement, for it was a deliberate statement on the part of the Finance Minister

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: Does any one deny it V

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: I deny it, the statement was not made. The statement made was that it was time enough when the government proposed to parliament.any scheme for aid, to discuss the condition under which that aid could be granted.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: No, the statement was that it was time enough when the Grand Trunk Pacific asked for assistance-and I will go further and say to hon. gentlemen on that side that they understood it in that light. The hon. member for Brant (Mr. Heyd)-if I may be permitted to use his name

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: Do not use my name, for I do not know anything about it.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
That hon. gentleman said in the committee that it did not make any difference to us where they built the railway so long as they paid for the construction of it. Therefore it had a perfect right to grant that legislation. That was the statement he made, and it was a misleading statement. There were other ministers of the Crown in attendance at that committee from tirpe to time, and from time to time this question was asked and answered in the w'ay and' spirit I have stated, and by reason of the answers given on different occasions to the committee, we refrained from discussing "'here that railway should run. Now the right hon. gentleman says to-night: is there anything in that correspondence that would be of service to members of the opposition ?
I hold that if members of the opposition and members of the government side who belong to the Railway Committee had/ known about that petition, they would have discussed the question from a different standpoint. I would ask the Finance Minister and the Prime Minister as well, what would have been the result after eight months of a session last year, if the legislation granted by this House had been carried out ? Would we in that case have heard anything of that petition to-night ? Not one word. Then again, the Finance Minister says that the object of reading that petition to-night was to meet the arguments presented by hon. gentlemen on this side.

But the same arguments were presented If st year. This subject is discussed throughout the country and every man who knows anything about it knows that the Grand Trunk last year expected that they would get fair and reasonable assistance in carrying out their project. That is what we believed then, and that is what we believe now. But when it was stated that no land grant was asked for by the company, then. I say again, the government were misleading the House. In the discussions that have taken place upon the land grants the Conservative opposition here have been taunted with supporting a policy of land grants to railways. But the government did not explain to us that the company last year were asking for $53,358,000 in land and money to assist the Grand Trunk Pacific. They misled the House with regard to this project. And I say it is a sorry finish to this affair when we find the government which preaches such a high standard of morality now, at the eleventh hour-no, not at the eleventh hour but at the twelfth hour and even longer after-reading a petition that was intended just as much for this country as for the government.

speakeroldname: Mr. ROBERT A. PRINGLE (Cornwall and Stormont).
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance has said that the reason why this document was not brought down before was that it had not been dealt with by the government. This document is signed by George A. Cox, Charles M. Hays and William Wainwright. Are we to understand that the government thought so little of these petitioners, and regarded their petition as of so little importance that they did not even consider it ? That does not seem to me to be reasonable. Another reason given by the Minister of Finance is that the document was marked 'confidential.' This memorial was addressed not to one individual member of the government, but the government as a whole. And this petition was followed almost immediately by the official notice in the * Canada Gazette.' The petition is dated November 2. 1902, and it was followed on December 15, 1902, by notice of application for the incorporation of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, the notice being almost in the very terms of the memorial. Hon. gentlemen opposite are not always so scrupulous with regard to documents that might be considered confidential. It was only the other evening that we had the Minister of Labour (Sir Wm. Mulock), when dealing with a discussion in regard to the alien labour, making the statement that Mr. Hays, instead of answering his correspondence had sent a letter marked ' confidential ' to the Prime Minister, that the document was a public one, and so he had no hesitation in telling the House the contents of it. And he went further, and said that his reason for being ready to give
it was that the Prime Minister had stated the'substance of it in the afternoon. This was the very foundation, the very initial proceeding, in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the parliament of this country was entitled to know how the proceedings were commenced.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: My only justification for addressing the House at this late hour of the morning is that there seems to be a misunderstanding between the two sides of the House with regard to the matter before us. As the hon. member for Cornwall (Mr. Pringle) has said, the government is formally committed to the principle that if a document is addressed to the government in a matter touching the public, even though marked ' private and confidential,' it is to be brought down.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
Documents have been brought down by the Postmaster General which were marked ' confidential,' and the plaudits of hon. gentlemen opposite supported him in doing so, while the Prime Minister had not a word to say against that course. The government, I think, laid down a principle, and I am not prepared to say that they have departed from it, that if a document relates to the public, even though marked ' confidential.' it should be brought down. It will be seen that this document relates to a matter in which the public has no concern whatever. We have only to look into the letter of Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson to see that. He says :
It has always seemed to me that the government of Canada

not the public of Canada, but the government of Canada,
-and the Grand Trunk Railway Company, being in point of fact partners in the enterprise-
And so on. I am prepared to defend the government in the position they have taken. They agree with Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson, that the position they occupy is that of a partner with the Grand Trunk in this great scheme, and they regard a communication from the head of the firm to the junior partner as confidential. True, it may relate. to a great public enterprise, but it is a matter in which the Grand Trunk and the government are partners. Evidently the hon. member for Cornwall and those behind him think that the public have something to do with these matters. This is a matter where the Bill conceived by the Prime Minister and arranged with the Grand Trunk is to be carried out. And, with the principle laid down by the government that, where the public is concerned, even a document marked ' confidential ' should be laid before the House, I am sure

they would have brought down everything that related to the public. The Prime Minister was quite sincere. Viewing this as a communication between partners, and one with which the public had nothing to do, the Prime Minister told us that everything was brought down that should be brought down. If that view is correct, that the public had nothing to do with this matter, they are perfectly right in refusing to bring down the document.
If the view held by hon. gentlemen on this side be correct the public is most intimately and vitally interested in this and is entitled to all the information it can have. Put while I would be sorry to say that the government are two-faced and brought down a document when it suited them, and did not when it did not suit them, still, if the government really believed that the public was interested in this matter they would have brought this document dowil. I think I am justified in saying it is a simple case of difference of opinion, the government and its supporters, as junior members of this important firm. Hays, Cox & Company, they should stand by their partners while we stood by the people.

subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Pringle) has alluded to me and stated that a short time ago I read in this House communications sent by Mr. Hays to the premier marked ' confidential.' 1 presume that, however inaccurate he may be, he has reference to some remarks which I made in the House upon the 13th of May instant. On that occasion I was giving to the House the correspondence up to date that had passed between myself and the Grand Trunk with reference to the subject that evening under discussion and stated that I had written to Mr. Hays and that he had replied transmitting to me a letter which he had sent to the premier which might properly have been sent to myself, and that Mr. Hays in his communication to me expressed the wish that I should not make his letter public except with the consent of the premier. He did not say to me that it might not be used by the premier, and the premier himself having the control of the document stated to the House before I spoke what its tenor was. When I spoke therefore. I did not make known to the House the nature of the letter to the premier ; the premier had already, as was his right, made that communication to the House.
Another hon. gentleman has referred to an incident that happened seven years ago when I published to the House and the country certain documents that were upon the public files when I took office. On that occasion the facts connected with the transaction were essentially different from those referred to to-night. On that occasion, I may say briefly that although I shared the entire Mr. NORTHRUP.
responsibility of that publication I had not myself seen the communications until they were printed and placed before the public. The matter came up incidentally in my department in the following method : One of the officers in the department asked me what was to be the procedure in dealing with public contracts and I told him the ordinary procedure that the law laid down. He informed me that that had not been the procedure in the past and brought to my knowledge a number of cases in which the public interest had been disregarded for the promotion of private interests, and on exa rnina-tion it was found that in these various transactions the irregular letting of contracts had resulted in a loss to the country of many hundreds of thousands of dollars, the exact figures of which I set forth in that report.
I gave instructions throughout the department that ail contracts that had been irregularly let were to be cancelled and relet according to the Post Office Act. That was done and I instructed that one of the officers of the department should prepare a return to parliament setting forth all the circumstances connected with the letting of these contracts and to give to parliament the correspondence bearing on the subject. I myself did not go into the public files or see the letters in advance of their publication, but they were published because the officer found them upon the public files. They were not placed upon the public files by me but by my predecessor, a member of the preceding administration, and I presume if he placed them on the public file it is fair to conclude that he had authority from the senders to so make use of them, and whether or not he had authority it seems to me that these letters had direct bearing upon the public affairs of the country, and disclosed and were part and parcel of, a project to rob the people of Canada. That is what they were and I doubt myself if the documents having that purport may be regarded as confidential. When my hon. friends opposite took extreme exception on that occasion to the course pursued I wonder how they reconciled their action then with their action to-night. Here they declare that no communication to a minister concerning the public interest should be regarded as private and confidential. How do they reconcile their contention to-night with their criticism of my actions seven years ago in having given to the public documents which I found on the public files ? That was the transaction then and I accept the full responsibility, but there is an essential difference between that transaction and the one to-night. In my case the documents were on a public file. I got them where they had been placed by my predecessor, in a very different method from that in which the leader of the opposition became possessed of a private and confidential document a short time ago, the circum-

stances of -which have not yet been satisfactorily explained to this House and to the country.
Amendment (Mr. Porter) negatived on the same division.

I move, seconded by Mr. Wilson :
That all the words after the word " That " in the main motion be left out and the following subtituted therefor :-' the Bill be referred back to a Committee of the Whole with instructions to amend the same by adding thereto the following as section No. - :-
" ' Notwithstanding anything in the scheduled agreements, or in this Act, or in the Act hereby amended contained, it is hereby declared and enacted that in the event of the government determining to undertake the operation of the Eastern Division upon the termination of the said lease, the government shall be entitled for a further period of fifty years to such running powers and haulage rights over the Western Division, or any portion thereof, and over any branch line or lines running from any point or points in the Eastern Division as may be necessary or expedient in the opinion of the government, upon such terms as may be agreed upon between the government and the Pacific Company, or as may from time to time in case of failure to so agree be determined in the manner provided by clause 24 (2) of the original agreement, which is hereby made applicable to cases arising under this section.' "
I moved this before, and it was understood that I would have the privilege of withdrawing it and moving it again to-day. I understood that the Minister of Justice desired to say something in connection with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: GEO. A. COX, CHAS. M. HAYS, WM. WAINWRIGHT.
speechtext:

I desired at the time to have an opportunity to look into what I had already said on the subject, for the purpose of deciding whether or not I would maintain the opinion I had then expressed. I have, since my hon. friend moved his amendment, considered the matter further, and I can see no reason to depart from the opinion I expressed when the amendment was moved in committee.
